title: Analysis of Algorithms
html:
Before writing a single data structure you need a way to say how fast and how much memory an algorithm uses without timing it on one particular computer. Asymptotic notation, loop analysis and recurrences are that language — every other topic in these notes ends with a line written in it.

Algorithm analysis — the process of determining the amount of time (time complexity) and memory (space complexity) an algorithm needs as a function of its input size n, independent of hardware, language or compiler.

Why analyse algorithms?

Predict before you build

Count operations on paper and you know whether a solution will finish for n = 10⁶ before implementing it — no benchmark needed.

Machine-independent

A faster laptop changes the constant, never the shape of the curve. O(n²) loses to O(n log n) on every machine once n is large enough.

Compare and choose

Two correct algorithms for the same problem are compared by their order of growth — the standard interview follow-up is always “can you do better?”.

Common vocabulary

“Linear”, “logarithmic”, “quadratic” are precise claims about how running time scales, understood by every engineer.

We count elementary operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic) rather than seconds, and we care about the order of growth — how the count scales when n doubles — not the exact number. Constants and lower-order terms are dropped: 3n² + 10n + 7 is simply O(n²).

Asymptotic notation: Big-O, Omega, Theta

Asymptotic analysis describes the growth of a function f(n) (the operation count) as n → ∞ by comparing it with a simpler function g(n). Three bounds are used:

Big-O — upper bound

f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. “It grows no faster than g.” This is what we usually quote.

Omega — lower bound

f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. “It grows at least as fast as g.” Used to prove problems need a minimum amount of work (comparison sorting is Ω(n log n)).

Theta — tight bound

f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀ — both O and Ω hold. “It grows exactly like g.”

f(n) = O(g(n)) ⇔ ∃ c > 0, n₀ : f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
Worked example

f(n) = 3n² + 10n + 7. For n ≥ 1, 10n ≤ 10n² and 7 ≤ 7n², so f(n) ≤ 20n² — pick c = 20, n₀ = 1 and f(n) = O(n²). Also f(n) ≥ 3n², so f(n) = Ω(n²), and therefore f(n) = Θ(n²).

Big-O is not “worst case”

O, Ω, Θ are bounds on a function; best case, worst case and average case are which input you analyse. They are independent: linear search is Θ(1) in the best case and Θ(n) in the worst case. When someone says “the algorithm is O(n²)” they almost always mean the worst-case running time is Θ(n²) — say which case you mean.

Key point

Because O is only an upper bound, n = O(n²) is technically true — but useless. Always give the tightest bound you can prove; that is why Θ is the honest answer in a proof and O is the everyday shorthand for it.

Big-O growth table

The classes below cover almost every algorithm you will meet, from fastest to slowest. The right-hand column is the rule of thumb for coding interviews and contests: roughly 10⁸ simple operations run in about a second.

Pitfall

Big-O hides constants, so for small n a “worse” algorithm can win: insertion sort (O(n²)) beats merge sort on arrays of 10–20 elements, which is exactly why library sorts switch to it for tiny sub-arrays. Big-O tells you what happens as n grows, not which program is faster on your input.

How to analyse a loop

Almost all non-recursive analysis reduces to one question per loop: how many times does the body run as a function of n? Then combine the loops with two rules.

1
Find the loop variable's path
Write down its start value, its stop condition and how it changes per iteration (+1, +k, ×2, squared…).
2
Solve for the iteration count
i = 0, 1, 2, … n−1 → n iterations. i = n, n−k, n−2k… → n/k. i = 1, 2, 4, 8 … n → log₂ n. i = 2, 2², 2⁴, 2⁸ … n → log log n.
3
Nested loops multiply
If the inner loop runs g(n) times for each of f(n) outer iterations, the total is f(n) · g(n). When the inner count depends on i, sum it: Σ i for i = 1..n is n(n+1)/2 = Θ(n²).
4
Sequential loops add
Loop A then loop B costs A + B; keep only the dominant term (n² + n = O(n²)), but keep both when sizes are independent (O(n + m)).
5
Charge the body
Multiply the iteration count by the cost of the body. A body that itself calls an O(log n) function inside an O(n) loop gives O(n log n).
6
Drop constants and lower-order terms
3n + 5 → O(n); n²/2 + n → O(n²). Keep the tightest class that remains.

Loop pattern: linear and fractional increments

The learner's original four examples are kept here, instrumented to print their iteration count so the complexity is visible. add decrements b by one per iteration, so it runs b times — O(b). subtract removes b from a per iteration, so it runs a / b times — still linear in a for a fixed b, because 1/b is a constant factor.

Time O(n) — n iterations, or n/k for a step of kSpace O(1)
Key point

Ten times the input → ten times the iterations: that proportionality is linear time. subtract(1000, 10) runs 100 times, not 1000, but the 1/10 is a constant and disappears in Big-O.

Loop pattern: logarithmic and log-log scaling

When the loop variable is multiplied by a constant c each round, it reaches n after log_c n rounds — a thousandfold larger input adds only a handful of iterations. When the variable is raised to a power each round (2 → 4 → 16 → 256 → 65536), the exponent itself doubles, so the loop runs log log n times — practically constant.

Time O(log n) for multiply, O(log log n) for exponentSpace O(1)
Key point

multiply(1000000, 2) needs only 20 rounds and exponent(10⁹, 2) only 5. Whenever you see a loop variable that halves or doubles — binary search, heap sift, exponentiation by squaring — think log n.

Loop pattern: nested and sequential loops

Nested loops multiply; loops one after another add. The program below counts the body executions of three classic nestings for n = 8 so you can match each count to its formula.

Time O(n²), O(n²), O(n log n), O(n) respectivelySpace O(1)
Pitfall

“The inner loop starts at i, so it is only half the work — O(n²/2), which is better.” It is not: n²/2 is Θ(n²). Halving a quadratic leaves a quadratic; only a change in the shape (e.g. doubling instead of incrementing) changes the class.

Recurrence relations for recursive algorithms

A recursive algorithm's running time is defined in terms of itself: the cost of the current call plus the cost of the recursive calls it makes. Writing that down gives a recurrence relation; solving it gives the complexity.

Recurrence relation — an equation that expresses T(n), the time for input size n, in terms of T on smaller inputs plus the work done outside the recursive calls, with a base case such as T(1) = Θ(1). Example: merge sort is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n).

AlgorithmRecurrenceWhat it saysSolution
Linear recursion (sum of n numbers, factorial)T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(1)one call of size n−1, constant workΘ(n)
Binary searchT(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1)one call on half the inputΘ(log n)
Merge sortT(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)two halves plus a linear mergeΘ(n log n)
Selection sort written recursivelyT(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(n)one smaller call plus a linear scanΘ(n²)
Tower of HanoiT(n) = 2T(n−1) + Θ(1)two calls on n−1 discsΘ(2ⁿ)
Naive FibonacciT(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + Θ(1)two calls, barely smallerΘ(φⁿ) ≈ Θ(1.618ⁿ)
Strassen matrix multiplyT(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²)seven half-size productsΘ(n^log₂7) ≈ Θ(n^2.81)

Three methods solve a recurrence:

Substitution method

Guess the answer (e.g. T(n) = O(n log n)), then prove it by induction: assume it holds for all smaller sizes, substitute into the recurrence, and show it still holds for n. Rigorous but needs a good guess.

Recursion tree method

Draw the calls as a tree. Write the non-recursive work at every node, sum each level, then sum the levels. It makes the guess for substitution obvious and is the way to see why merge sort is n log n.

Master method

A template for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) with n^(log_b a) and read off the answer. Covers most divide-and-conquer algorithms in one line.

Recursion tree: why merge sort is n log n

For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n every level of the tree does n work in total — the input is split in half but there are twice as many pieces. There are log₂ n levels of splitting plus the leaves, so the total is n · (log₂ n + 1) = Θ(n log n).

The program below evaluates that recurrence exactly for powers of two and prints the total next to the closed form — the two columns agree at every size.

Time Θ(n log n) — the recurrence's solutionSpace O(log n) recursion depth

Master theorem

For divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1 subproblems each of size n/b (b > 1), the answer depends on which wins: the leaves (n^(log_b a) of them, each Θ(1)) or the root's work f(n).

T(n) = a · T(n / b) + f(n) — compare f(n) with n^(log_b a)

2 — balancedf(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a))every level does the same work; there are log n levelsT(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n)
3 — root dominatesf(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) and a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c < 1f(n) is polynomially larger; the top call does most of the workT(n) = Θ(f(n))

1
Identify a, b, f(n)
a = number of recursive calls, b = the factor the input shrinks by, f(n) = the work done outside the calls (splitting, merging, scanning).
2
Compute the critical exponent
p = log_b a. Examples: a = 2, b = 2 → p = 1; a = 4, b = 2 → p = 2; a = 1, b = 2 → p = 0.
3
Compare f(n) with n^p
Smaller by a polynomial factor → case 1. Equal → case 2. Larger by a polynomial factor → case 3 (check regularity).
4
Read off T(n)
Θ(n^p), Θ(n^p log n) or Θ(f(n)).
When it does not apply

The master theorem does not apply when the sub-problems are not of size n/b (T(n) = T(n−1) + … — use the recursion tree or unroll by hand), when a < 1, or when f(n) differs from n^(log_b a) by less than a polynomial factor (n log n vs n is only a log apart — a gap between cases 2 and 3). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n is the standard trap.

Space complexity vs auxiliary space

TermWhat is countedExample: sum an array of n numbers iteratively
Space complexityall memory the algorithm needs — the input itself plus any extraO(n) — the array has to be there
Auxiliary spaceonly the extra memory beyond the input: temporaries, new arrays, hash maps, the recursion stackO(1) — one accumulator

Interviewers nearly always mean auxiliary space when they ask “what is the space complexity?”, because it is what distinguishes solutions: sorting in place is O(1) auxiliary, merge sort's buffer is O(n), and a recursive solution pays for its call stack. Recursion is the classic hidden cost — each pending call keeps a frame alive until it returns.

Example

Input: n = 5
Output: sum = 15, deepest call stack = 6 frames (n + 1: the base-case call add_recursion(0) is a frame too)

Time O(n) time for bothSpace O(n) auxiliary (recursive) vs O(1) (iterative)
Pitfall

Counting the recursion stack is the step most people forget: the recursive sum looks like it uses no memory, yet n + 1 frames are alive at the deepest point. Python stops at about 1000 frames with RecursionError; C++ and Java crash with a stack overflow a few thousand frames later. Depth, not the number of calls, is what costs space — a function that makes 2ⁿ calls but is never more than n deep uses O(n) stack.

Interview Q&A

What is the difference between Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta?

O(g) is an upper bound (grows no faster than g), Ω(g) a lower bound (grows at least as fast), Θ(g) a tight bound (both). All three are statements about a function's growth, not about best or worst case. In everyday use “O(n log n)” is shorthand for “the worst case is Θ(n log n)”.

Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms?

Because they depend on the machine, the compiler and the exact operation mix — and because for large n they do not change which algorithm wins: 100n beats n² as soon as n > 100. Asymptotic notation captures what survives all those details: the shape of the growth curve. Constants still matter when choosing between two algorithms of the same class.

Can an O(n²) algorithm be faster than an O(n log n) one?

Yes, for small inputs or when the constant factors differ a lot. Insertion sort beats merge sort below roughly 20 elements, which is why production sorts (Timsort, introsort) switch to it for small sub-arrays. Big-O describes behaviour as n → ∞, not the timing of a particular run.

How do you find the time complexity of nested loops?

Count the body executions: multiply independent loop counts (n × n = n²), sum dependent ones (Σ (n − i) = n(n+1)/2 = Θ(n²)), and multiply by the body's own cost. Watch the increment: i += 1 gives n, i *= 2 gives log n, i = i² gives log log n.

What is the master theorem and when can you not use it?

For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) it compares f(n) with n^(log_b a): polynomially smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)); equal → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n); polynomially larger (with the regularity condition) → Θ(f(n)). It does not apply to subtract-and-conquer recurrences like T(n−1), to a < 1, or when f(n) and n^(log_b a) differ by only a logarithmic factor (2T(n/2) + n log n), which needs the extended version or a recursion tree.

What is the difference between space complexity and auxiliary space?

Space complexity counts everything including the input; auxiliary space counts only the extra memory the algorithm allocates — temporaries, new containers and the recursion stack. Interviewers mean auxiliary space: an in-place sort is O(1), merge sort is O(n), and a recursive function is at least O(depth).

What is amortised analysis?

Averaging the cost of an operation over a long sequence rather than looking at the worst single call. Appending to a dynamic array occasionally costs O(n) to resize, but doubling the capacity makes the total for n appends O(n), so each append is amortised O(1). It is a guarantee about the sequence, not a probability — unlike average-case analysis.
